metadata.title: Does between-school tracking really result in more achievement homogeneous schools? Evidence from 40 countries around the globe
metadata.venue: Research in Social Stratification and Mobility

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available ILSA microdata from PIRLS 2011, TIMSS 2011 (Grade 4), and PISA 2018, and then restricts the analytic sample to 40 countries (or subnational entities) with sufficient PISA population coverage (≥80%) and with available tracking-age information. For Stage 1 multilevel variance decomposition, the authors state that Mplus implements large-scale assessment weighting in multilevel situations and that school weight is used as the Level 2 weight, while no weight is used at Level 1 (per their cited procedure). This implies complex survey weighting is applied at the school level to obtain variance components (WSAV/BSAV) that are representative within each country. The manuscript does not report the exact weight variable name(s), and it does not use replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight-based uncertainty estimation is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper explicitly states that achievement scores used to compute WSAV/BSAV are based on plausible values, but it does not report the missing-data strategy for the retained variables (e.g., whether cases with missing PVs or covariates were excluded, or whether multiple imputation was used). This is a reporting gap because ILSA datasets typically require a documented approach to missing responses and PV-related missingness to ensure reproducibility of variance decomposition and effect-size standard errors. The authors also do not provide enough methodological detail to determine whether missingness was handled via listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample includes only countries (or subnational entities) that participated in either (PIRLS 2011 + PISA 2018) or (TIMSS 2011 + PISA 2018), yielding 40 countries total. For comparability, the authors restrict PISA to the same subnational parts used in PIRLS/TIMSS (e.g., only Alberta/Ontario/Quebec for Canada; only England and Northern Ireland for the UK; only Flemish Belgium for TIMSS–PISA and only French Belgium for PIRLS–PISA). Countries are further restricted to those with PISA population coverage ≥80% (excluding Bulgaria, Colombia, Morocco, Romania, Thailand, and Turkey), and Saudi Arabia is excluded because no age-of-selection data were available. Additionally, students are restricted to the relevant cohorts: PIRLS/TIMSS Grade 4 (age ~10) and PISA 2018 age 15 (with pseudo-panel logic using students born around 2001/2002). Students who participated in both PIRLS and TIMSS are counted once.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis: WSAV change μ̂ = -10.19 (95% CI [-16.96, -3.42]); mixed-effects moderation: early vs late B = 16.74 (p = .055, QM(2)=5.73).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 & PISA 2018 reading data (Grade 4 vs age 15), the study leveraged tracking age group to estimate WSAV change, finding that WSAV decreased on average (μ̂ = -10.19) and that the early-tracking advantage for WSAV reduction was statistically significant in the general early-tracking comparison for reading (p < .05). This indicates that earlier between-school tracking produces only limited within-school homogenization, so policy should not assume that tracking automatically yields more achievement-homogeneous classrooms.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis: BSAV change μ̂ = 10.27 (95% CI [3.37, 17.15]); mixed-effects moderation: early vs late B = -28.50 (p < .05, QM(2)=12.11, R²=12.5%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 & PISA 2018 reading data (Grade 4 vs age 15), the study leveraged tracking age group to estimate BSAV change, finding that BSAV increased on average (μ̂ = 10.27) and that the increase was significantly larger in early-tracking than in late-tracking countries (B = -28.50, p < .05). This indicates that while tracking may slightly reduce within-school variation, it substantially widens between-school achievement gaps, implying that tracking reforms should be paired with strong measures to improve instruction in lower tracks.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis: WSAV change μ̂ = -7.20 (95% CI [-13.00, -1.41]); mixed-effects moderation: early vs late B = 7.81 (p = .339, QM(2)=2.26, R²=0.3%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 & PISA 2018 math data (Grade 4 vs age 15), the study leveraged tracking age group to estimate WSAV change, finding that WSAV decreased on average (μ̂ = -7.20) but that tracking did not significantly moderate WSAV change between early- and late-tracking countries (B = 7.81, p = .339). This indicates that between-school tracking is not reliably effective at increasing within-school achievement homogeneity in mathematics, so instructional differentiation remains necessary.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis: BSAV change μ̂ = 7.16 (95% CI [-0.45, 14.76]); mixed-effects moderation: early vs late B = -27.36 (p < .05, QM(2)=8.49, R²=8.3%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 & PISA 2018 math data (Grade 4 vs age 15), the study leveraged tracking age group to estimate BSAV change, finding that BSAV increased and that the increase was significantly larger in early-tracking than in late-tracking countries (B = -27.36, p < .05). This indicates that tracking tends to amplify between-school inequality in math, suggesting that policy should focus on reducing track-related instructional disparities rather than expecting homogenization.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis: WSAV change μ̂ = -5.01 (95% CI [-12.46, -2.44]); mixed-effects moderation: early vs late B = 16.05 (p = .102, QM(2)=7.45, R²=6.9%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 & PISA 2018 science data (Grade 4 vs age 15), the study leveraged tracking age group to estimate WSAV change, finding that WSAV decreased on average (μ̂ = -5.01) and that tracking significantly moderated WSAV change in the general model (QM(2)=7.45, p < .05) though domain-specific early vs late differences were not significant at conventional levels (B = 16.05, p = .102). This indicates that within-school homogenization from tracking is weak and domain-dependent, so science instruction should still be designed for heterogeneous learners.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random-effects meta-analysis: BSAV change μ̂ = 5.12 (95% CI [-3.40, 13.64]); mixed-effects moderation: early vs late B = -30.60 (p < .05, QM(2)=10.45, R²=10.1%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 & PISA 2018 science data (Grade 4 vs age 15), the study leveraged tracking age group to estimate BSAV change, finding that BSAV increased and that the increase was significantly larger in early-tracking than in late-tracking countries (B = -30.60, p < .05). This indicates that early between-school tracking is associated with widening between-school achievement gaps in science, implying that reforms should prioritize equalizing instructional quality across tracks.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses a two-stage individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis combining TIMSS 2011 (Grade 4) and PIRLS 2011 with PISA 2018 to create a pseudo-panel DID design across 40 countries (631,368 students). In Stage 1, multilevel variance decomposition in Mplus estimates within-school achievement variation (WSAV) and between-school achievement variation (BSAV) for reading, math, and science, using plausible values and school-level weighting. In Stage 2, random- and mixed-effects meta-regressions synthesize country-level WSAV/BSAV change from age ~10 to age 15 and test moderation by tracking regime (early 10–12, mid 14–15, late 16). Results show small average WSAV reductions (significant mainly for reading/general models) but marked BSAV increases in early-tracking countries, with tracking explaining about 8.3–12.5% of between-country BSAV-change variance. Limitations include the pseudo-panel/DID assumptions, relative (standardized) variance interpretation, and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling.
